:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Express $2\cos^2{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}-1$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
2 \cos^2 x - 1 = \cos 2x
$$

Substituting $x={\dfrac{\pi}{3}}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)-1 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Express $5-10{\sin }^{2}⁡{20}^{∘}$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Our expression can be factored as follows:

$$
5(1-2{\sin }^{2}⁡{20}^{∘})
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
1-2{\sin }^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x={20}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1-2{\sin }^{2}⁡{20}^{∘} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot {20}^{∘})=\operatorname{cos}⁡{40}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
5(1-2{\sin }^{2}⁡{20}^{∘})=5\operatorname{cos}⁡{40}^{∘}.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Express $2\cos^2(26^\circ)-1$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Use the alternative cosine double-angle formula:

$$
2\cos^2 x-1=\cos(2x).
$$

Substitute $x=26^\circ$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\cos^2(26^\circ)-1&=\cos(2\cdot26^\circ)\\
&=\cos(52^\circ).
\end{aligned}
$$

The angle doubles; the result has no square or extra factor of $2$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Express $3-6\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{10}\right)$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First factor out $3$ to expose the identity:

$$
3-6\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{10}\right)=3\left(1-2\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{10}\right)\right).
$$

Use the alternative cosine double-angle formula:

$$
1-2\sin^2 x=\cos(2x).
$$

With $x=\frac{\pi}{10}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\left(1-2\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{10}\right)\right)&=3\cos\left(2\cdot\frac{\pi}{10}\right)\\
&=3\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The outside factor $3$ remains; only the angle inside the cosine doubles.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Express $8\cos^4(18^\circ)-8\cos^2(18^\circ)+1$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Regroup the expression so that the alternative double-angle formula can be used twice. To check the regrouping, write $u=\cos^2(18^\circ)$:

$$
2(2u-1)^2-1=2(4u^2-4u+1)-1=8u^2-8u+1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&8\cos^4(18^\circ)-8\cos^2(18^\circ)+1\\
&\qquad=2\left(2\cos^2(18^\circ)-1\right)^2-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use $2\cos^2 x-1=\cos(2x)$ first at $x=18^\circ$:

$$
2\cos^2(18^\circ)-1=\cos(36^\circ).
$$

Substitute this into the regrouped expression, then use the same identity at $x=36^\circ$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\left(2\cos^2(18^\circ)-1\right)^2-1&=2\cos^2(36^\circ)-1\\
&=\cos(2\cdot36^\circ)\\
&=\cos(72^\circ).
\end{aligned}
$$

Both applications are needed: $\cos(36^\circ)$ replaces only the inner expression.
